items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs (Brundtland Report, 1987)”?
items.answer: Sustainable development
items.markingKey: Sustainable development: development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs (Brundtland Report, 1987). [1]

items.stem: Explain why there can be conflict between economic development and environmental sustainability.
items.answer: Economic growth often relies on resource extraction, fossil fuels and land conversion, causing pollution and habitat loss; environmental protection may raise costs or limit jobs in the short term.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed point up to [3]

items.stem: Explain how the triple bottom line can be used to evaluate a development project.
items.answer: The project is judged on its social impacts (jobs, health, communities), environmental impacts (pollution, habitats, emissions) and economic impacts (profit, income); a sustainable project performs well on all three.
items.markingKey: three elements explained [2]; application [1] [3]

items.stem: In a lower-middle-income country, the percentage of the population that is undernourished was 28% in 2010 and 26% in 2020. This is an indicator for SDG 2 (zero hunger). Suggest why progress may slow as the indicator approaches the target.
items.answer: The remaining people are hardest to reach: remote rural areas, the poorest groups and conflict zones, where costs are highest.

items.stem: In Country B, the percentage of the population with access to electricity was 62% in 2012 and 80% in 2022. This is an indicator for SDG 7 (affordable and clean energy). (a) Calculate the mean change in percentage points per year. (b) Assuming this rate continues, determine whether the country will reach the target of 100% by 2030.
items.answer: (a) 1.80 per year (b) It would reach 100% in about 2033, so it is not on track.

items.stem: Assess the extent to which sustainable development is an unachievable goal. Support your answer with examples. In your answer you should consider: named projects; decoupling; SDGs.
items.answer: For: Global resource use exceeds biocapacity; emissions are still rising; many SDG targets are off track for 2030; there are conflicts between growth and protection. Against: Many countries have decoupled growth from emissions (e.g. the UK, Sweden); renewable energy is growing quickly; local projects (agroforestry, ecotourism) show sustainable development in practice. Judgement: Full sustainability is difficult but progress is possible; it is better seen as a direction of travel than a fixed end point.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (6-8 marks): detailed, balanced discussion using named examples and data, with a reasoned judgement. Level 2 (3-5 marks): developed points but limited balance or exemplification. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generalised points. [8]

items.answer: It would reach 100% in about 2122, so it is not on track.

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a formal process to predict and evaluate the environmental effects of a proposed development before a decision is made”?
items.answer: Environmental impact assessment (EIA)
items.markingKey: Environmental impact assessment (EIA): a formal process to predict and evaluate the environmental effects of a proposed development before a decision is made. [1]

items.stem: Describe the main stages of an environmental impact assessment.
items.answer: Screening; scoping of key impacts; baseline survey; prediction and evaluation of impacts; mitigation measures; public consultation; environmental impact statement; decision; monitoring after approval.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage in order up to [4]

items.stem: Explain the importance of public consultation in an EIA.
items.answer: Local people know the area and may identify impacts experts miss; it allows stakeholders to raise concerns and influence decisions; it increases transparency and acceptance of the project.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [3]

items.stem: A company proposes a new coastal resort on a mangrove-fringed bay in the Philippines, with a hotel, a marina and a golf course. Explain why monitoring should continue after construction.
items.answer: To check that predicted impacts were accurate and mitigation is working, and to detect unexpected impacts.

items.stem: A government is considering a proposal to build a large hydroelectric dam in the middle hills of Nepal that would flood 120 km² of forested valley, including two villages, to supply electricity and water for irrigation. (a) Explain why an environmental impact assessment is needed for this project. (b) Explain why monitoring should continue after construction.
items.answer: (a) It is a large project with potentially significant impacts on habitats, water, and communities; the EIA identifies and evaluates impacts and mitigation before a decision is made. (b) To check that predicted impacts were accurate and mitigation is working, and to detect unexpected impacts.

items.stem: A company proposes a new coastal resort on a mangrove-fringed bay in coastal Kenya, with a hotel, a marina and a golf course. (a) Explain why an environmental impact assessment is needed for this project. (b) Explain why monitoring should continue after construction.
items.answer: (a) It is a large project with potentially significant impacts on habitats, water, and communities; the EIA identifies and evaluates impacts and mitigation before a decision is made. (b) To check that predicted impacts were accurate and mitigation is working, and to detect unexpected impacts.

items.stem: A student writes: “An EIA decides whether a project goes ahead.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. The EIA informs decision-makers; the decision is made by a government or planning authority, which may approve projects with significant impacts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Part of an impact matrix for a wind farm gives each impact a magnitude (−5 to +5) and an importance (1 to 5). The score for each factor is magnitude × importance. water quality: magnitude −3, importance 1; landscape: magnitude −4, importance 4; soil: magnitude −4, importance 1; traffic: magnitude −5, importance 1. Explain two limitations of using an impact matrix.
items.answer: Scores are subjective and may be biased; very different impacts are added as if equal; indirect and cumulative impacts are hard to score; it does not show who is affected.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A government is considering a proposal to build a large hydroelectric dam in the Cordillera of the Philippines that would flood 120 km² of forested valley, including two villages, to supply electricity and water for irrigation. items.answer: (a) It is a large project with potentially significant impacts on habitats, water, and communities; the EIA identifies and evaluates impacts and mitigation before a decision is made. (b) To check that predicted impacts were accurate and mitigation is working, and to detect unexpected impacts.

items.stem: A government is considering a proposal to build a large hydroelectric dam in the Western Ghats of India that would flood 120 km² of forested valley, including two villages, to supply electricity and water for irrigation. (a) Identify three stakeholders and suggest the view of each. (b) Explain why monitoring should continue after construction.
items.answer: (a) Local residents (concern over displacement or loss of livelihoods; possible jobs); developer or company (profit, wants approval); environmental NGOs (concern for habitats); government (economic growth, energy or tourism revenue). (b) To check that predicted impacts were accurate and mitigation is working, and to detect unexpected impacts.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per stakeholder with view [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the order of preference for managing waste: prevent and reduce, reuse, recycle, recover energy, and finally disposal”?
items.answer: Waste hierarchy
items.markingKey: Waste hierarchy: the order of preference for managing waste: prevent and reduce, reuse, recycle, recover energy, and finally disposal. [1]

items.stem: Explain the environmental problems caused by landfill sites.
items.answer: Leachate pollutes groundwater and rivers; methane is released, contributing to climate change and fire risk; land is used up; odour, pests and litter; plastics persist for centuries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per problem up to [3]

items.stem: Evaluate incineration as a method of waste disposal.
items.answer: Advantages: reduces waste volume by about 90%; generates electricity or heat; less land needed. Disadvantages: emits CO₂ and pollutants such as dioxins if poorly controlled; toxic ash must be disposed of; may discourage recycling; expensive to build.
items.markingKey: advantages [1-2]; disadvantages [1-2] [4]

items.stem: For Lagos, Nigeria or another example of a waste management strategy, briefly evaluate the sustainability of the waste management strategy.
items.answer: Lagos, Nigeria: Collection has improved in wealthier districts, but much waste is dumped in drains and lagoons, causing flooding; dumpsite fires release toxic smoke; informal waste pickers face health risks.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. environmental, social, economic outcomes; judgement [4]

items.stem: Refer to your case study of a waste management strategy (for example Sweden). Briefly describe the strategies used to manage waste.
items.answer: Sweden: Landfill taxes and a ban on landfilling organic and combustible waste; extensive recycling, deposit schemes for bottles and cans; about half of household waste is burned in energy-from-waste plants supplying district heating.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. named methods, scale, data [4]

items.stem: Name an example of a waste management strategy. For your chosen example, evaluate the sustainability of the waste management strategy.
items.answer: Model answer (Sweden): Less than 1% of household waste goes to landfill; but incineration emits CO₂, and Sweden imports waste to keep plants running, which may discourage waste reduction.

items.stem: A student writes: “All plastics are easily recycled.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many plastics are mixed, contaminated or low value; only about 9% of plastic ever produced has been recycled.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: A European city has 600 000 people, each producing 0.8 kg of municipal solid waste per day. 45% is recycled, 5% is composted and the rest is landfilled. The landfill site has 2 million m³ of space left and compacted waste has a density of 0.8 t/m³. (a) Calculate the mass of waste sent to landfill each year. (b) Calculate the new lifetime if the recycling rate increases to 60%.

A city in Indonesia has 250 000 people, each producing 1.5 kg of municipal solid waste per day. 10% is recycled, 5% is composted and the rest is landfilled. The landfill site has 2 million m³ of space left and compacted waste has a density of 0.8 t/m³. (a) Calculate the mass of waste sent to landfill each year. (b) Calculate the remaining lifetime of the landfill site. (c) Suggest two ways the city could increase its recycling rate.
items.answer: (a) 116 344 t (b) 13.8 years (c) Separate kerbside collections; deposit-return schemes; landfill taxes; support and formalise waste pickers; education campaigns; recycling centres.

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a non-profit organisation independent of government, such as WWF, Greenpeace or Friends of the Earth”?

items.stem: Explain why international agreements are needed to solve some environmental problems.
items.answer: Problems such as climate change, ozone depletion and ocean pollution cross borders; no single country can solve them; agreements share responsibility, avoid free-riding and coordinate action.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [3]

items.stem: Explain the roles of NGOs in environmental management.
items.answer: Campaigning and raising awareness; lobbying governments; carrying out research and monitoring; running conservation projects; working with local communities; holding companies to account.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per role up to [3]

items.stem: Under the Paris Agreement the United Kingdom pledged to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2030 compared with 2005. Emissions were 400 Mt CO₂e in 2005 and 320 Mt CO₂e in 2022. Calculate the average annual reduction needed from 2022 to 2030.
items.answer: 15.0 Mt CO₂e per year

items.stem: Under the Paris Agreement Country X pledged to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 45% by 2030 compared with 2005. Emissions were 400 Mt CO₂e in 2005 and 304 Mt CO₂e in 2022. (a) Calculate the target emissions for 2030. (b) Calculate the average annual reduction needed from 2022 to 2030.
items.answer: (a) 220 Mt CO₂e (b) 10.5 Mt CO₂e per year

items.stem: To what extent is it true that governments are more important than individuals in solving environmental problems?
items.answer: For: Governments can pass laws, set taxes and subsidies, invest in infrastructure and negotiate international agreements (Montreal Protocol, Paris Agreement). Against: Individuals change consumption, vote, protest (e.g. Fridays for Future) and support NGOs; without public support policies fail; NGOs and businesses also play key roles. Judgement: Governments have the greatest power, but they respond to pressure from individuals and NGOs; all levels must act together.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that environmental impact assessments are effective in protecting the environment from development?
items.answer: For: EIA has led to changes in project design, mitigation and sometimes cancellation; it gives the public a voice and creates baseline data. Against: EIAs are often biased, rushed or ignored; large projects such as the Belo Monte Dam in Brazil went ahead despite serious concerns; cumulative impacts are often missed; monitoring is weak. Judgement: EIA is valuable but its effectiveness depends on independent assessment, public participation and enforcement.

items.stem: Assess the extent to which recycling is the most sustainable way to manage waste. Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: Recycling saves raw materials and energy (aluminium recycling uses about 95% less energy), reduces landfill and creates jobs. Against: Reduction and reuse are higher in the waste hierarchy; recycling uses energy, often downcycles plastics and depends on markets; much is exported or not actually recycled. Judgement: Recycling is better than disposal but less sustainable than reducing and reusing; it works best within a circular economy.

items.stem: A government is considering a proposal to build a large hydroelectric dam in the Andes of Peru that would flood 120 km² of forested valley, including two villages, to supply electricity and water for irrigation. (a) Explain why an environmental impact assessment is needed for this project. (b) Identify three stakeholders and suggest the view of each. (c) Describe how a baseline survey of the area could be carried out.
items.answer: (a) It is a large project with potentially significant impacts on habitats, water, and communities; the EIA identifies and evaluates impacts and mitigation before a decision is made. (b) Local residents (concern over displacement or loss of livelihoods; possible jobs); developer or company (profit, wants approval); environmental NGOs (concern for habitats); government (economic growth, energy or tourism revenue). (c) Map habitats; quadrat and transect surveys of vegetation; bird and mammal counts; water quality and flow measurements; questionnaires with local people; air and noise measurements.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark per stakeholder with view [3] (c) 1 mark per method up to [3]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “landfill”?
options: The disposal of waste by burying it in the ground in a specially engineered site.
The controlled aerobic decomposition of organic waste to produce a soil conditioner.
The polluted liquid that drains from waste in a landfill site.
The burning of waste at high temperatures, often to generate electricity (energy from waste).
items.answer: The disposal of waste by burying it in the ground in a specially engineered site.
items.markingKey: Landfill: the disposal of waste by burying it in the ground in a specially engineered site. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “All plastics are easily recycled.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer. (b) Evaluate incineration as a method of waste disposal.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Many plastics are mixed, contaminated or low value; only about 9% of plastic ever produced has been recycled. (b) Advantages: reduces waste volume by about 90%; generates electricity or heat; less land needed. Disadvantages: emits CO₂ and pollutants such as dioxins if poorly controlled; toxic ash must be disposed of; may discourage recycling; expensive to build.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2] (b) advantages [1-2]; disadvantages [1-2] [4]

items.stem: A city in Mexico has 250 000 people, each producing 0.7 kg of municipal solid waste per day. 5% is recycled, 15% is composted and the rest is landfilled. The landfill site has 2 million m³ of space left and compacted waste has a density of 0.8 t/m³. Calculate the new lifetime if the recycling rate increases to 20%.
items.answer: 38.5 years
items.markingKey: landfilled 41 519 t/yr [1]; 38.5 years [1] [2]

items.stem: A city in Indonesia has 4 000 000 people, each producing 0.9 kg of municipal solid waste per day. 45% is recycled, 15% is composted and the rest is landfilled. The landfill site has 2 million m³ of space left and compacted waste has a density of 0.8 t/m³. (a) Calculate the remaining lifetime of the landfill site. (b) Suggest two ways the city could increase its recycling rate.
items.answer: (a) 3.04 years (b) Separate kerbside collections; deposit-return schemes; landfill taxes; support and formalise waste pickers; education campaigns; recycling centres.

items.stem: “Recycling is the most sustainable way to manage waste.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: Recycling saves raw materials and energy (aluminium recycling uses about 95% less energy), reduces landfill and creates jobs. Against: Reduction and reuse are higher in the waste hierarchy; recycling uses energy, often downcycles plastics and depends on markets; much is exported or not actually recycled. Judgement: Recycling is better than disposal but less sustainable than reducing and reusing; it works best within a circular economy.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 4 (10-12 marks): detailed, balanced evaluation supported by named examples and a clear, justified conclusion. Level 3 (7-9 marks): developed discussion with examples, judgement partly supported. Level 2 (4-6 marks): some relevant points, mostly descriptive. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, unsupported statements. [12]

items.stem: A news article states: “NGOs can pass environmental laws.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. NGOs can campaign and influence, but only governments and legislatures pass laws.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A student writes: “Individual actions make no difference to environmental problems.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why the Kyoto Protocol had limited success.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Collective individual choices (diet, transport, energy, consumption) add up and influence businesses and governments. (b) The USA never ratified it; developing countries including China and India had no binding targets; Canada withdrew; targets were small; global emissions continued to rise.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per reason up to [3]

items.stem: Under the Paris Agreement the European Union pledged to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 55% by 2030 compared with 1990. Emissions were 600 Mt CO₂e in 1990 and 420 Mt CO₂e in 2022. Suggest two policies the government could use to achieve this reduction.
items.answer: Carbon tax or emissions trading; subsidies for renewables and electric vehicles; phase-out of coal; building insulation standards; investment in public transport.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Under the Paris Agreement the European Union pledged to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 55% by 2030 compared with 2005. Emissions were 600 Mt CO₂e in 2005 and 450 Mt CO₂e in 2022. (a) Calculate the target emissions for 2030. (b) Explain why it is difficult to enforce targets under the Paris Agreement.
items.answer: (a) 270 Mt CO₂e (b) Targets (NDCs) are set by each country and are not legally binding; there are no penalties; countries can change their pledges or withdraw.

items.stem: Evaluate the view that governments are more important than individuals in solving environmental problems. In your answer you should consider: laws and taxes; NGOs.
items.answer: For: Governments can pass laws, set taxes and subsidies, invest in infrastructure and negotiate international agreements (Montreal Protocol, Paris Agreement). Against: Individuals change consumption, vote, protest (e.g. Fridays for Future) and support NGOs; without public support policies fail; NGOs and businesses also play key roles. Judgement: Governments have the greatest power, but they respond to pressure from individuals and NGOs; all levels must act together.
